explanations.answer: He'll be cheered to learn how they're doing
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul says he hopes to send Timothy soon, "…that I also may be cheered when I learn how you are doing." (Philippians 2:19) He hopes to be cheered by learning how the Philippians are doing. I know a little about wanting news from people you can't see.

explanations.answer: He'll get help preparing for his trial
explanations.explanation: Paul never says anything about a trial in this verse. He says he hopes Timothy's visit means he "…may be cheered when I learn how you are doing." (Philippians 2:19) What he names is learning how the Philippians are doing.

explanations.answer: He'll get supplies for his time in chains
explanations.explanation: Good guess, friend, but Paul doesn't mention supplies here. He says he hopes to send Timothy "…that I also may be cheered when I learn how you are doing." (Philippians 2:19) The verse names learning how the Philippians are doing.

Yes, baker! Paul says nobody else will "…genuinely care for your needs." (Philippians 2:20) Not care a little, not care when it's convenient. Genuinely. That's the kind of word you want said about you.

Close, but speaking isn't the word. Paul says Timothy is the one "…who will genuinely care for your needs." (Philippians 2:20) Talk is easy, friend. I could talk all day, and my mustache would still be the only one doing any work.

Paul doesn't say anything about paying here. The verse says Timothy "…will genuinely care for your needs." (Philippians 2:20) It's about caring, and a person's heart is worth more than their wallet. Timothy's heart is what Paul is bragging on.

Read it again, baker, because this one flips on you. Paul says, "For all the others look after their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ." (Philippians 2:21) So the others look after their own interests, not Christ's. Timothy is the one Paul sets apart from them.

Right, baker, the statement has it backwards. Paul says, "For all the others look after their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ." (Philippians 2:21) The others look after their own interests, not Christ's. Timothy is the one who stands apart from that.

explanations.answer: Like a child with his father
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Paul says Timothy "…as a child with his father he has served with me to advance the gospel." (Philippians 2:22) Paul and Timothy have a close bond. And the Philippians already know Timothy's proven worth.

explanations.answer: Like a soldier with his captain
explanations.explanation: Paul does use soldier language, but he uses it for Epaphroditus (Philippians 2:25), not for Timothy here. For Timothy, Paul says "…as a child with his father he has served with me to advance the gospel." (Philippians 2:22) Same work, but the picture is family.

explanations.answer: Like a servant with his master
explanations.explanation: That's a fair guess, friend, but it isn't the picture Paul paints. He says Timothy served with him "…as a child with his father…" (Philippians 2:22) A child and a father, working side by side to advance the gospel.

explanations.answer: As soon as he sees what happens with him
explanations.explanation: You've got it. Paul says, "So I hope to send him as soon as I see what happens with me." (Philippians 2:23) Paul is waiting to see how things go for him first. I wait on ovens all day, so I know a thing about waiting for the right moment.

explanations.answer: As soon as the Philippians write him back
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. Paul never says he's waiting on a letter from Philippi. He says he hopes to send Timothy "…as soon as I see what happens with me." (Philippians 2:23) The waiting is about what happens with Paul.

explanations.answer: As soon as he finishes writing this letter
explanations.explanation: Nice thinking, friend, since this whole passage is part of a letter. But the verse says something else: "…as soon as I see what happens with me." (Philippians 2:23) Paul is waiting to see what happens with him. Finishing the letter isn't the thing he names.
True, baker! Paul writes, "And I trust in the Lord that I myself will come soon." (Philippians 2:24) His trust is in the Lord. That's a good place for it.
That's an easy one to doubt, friend, but this one is true. Paul writes, "And I trust in the Lord that I myself will come soon." (Philippians 2:24) He trusts in the Lord that he'll come himself.

That's right, baker. Paul calls Epaphroditus "…your messenger and minister to my needs." (Philippians 2:25) He's the Philippians' messenger, and he's also looking after Paul. That's a man with two jobs and one big heart.

Look at the verse again, friend. Paul calls Epaphroditus "…your messenger and minister to my needs." (Philippians 2:25) So he's the Philippians' messenger, and he also ministers to Paul's needs. The statement is true.

explanations.answer: The Philippians heard he was ill
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! Paul says Epaphroditus "…has been longing for all of you and is distressed because you heard he was ill." (Philippians 2:26) He's the one who was ill, and he's distressed that they heard about it. I think that's a good heart on him.

Good guess, but that's not what the verse says. Paul says Epaphroditus "…is distressed because you heard he was ill." (Philippians 2:26) What troubles him is that the Philippians heard about his illness. It isn't a lack of news.

That's a heavy guess, friend, and the verse doesn't say it. Paul says Epaphroditus "…is distressed because you heard he was ill." (Philippians 2:26) The distress is about the Philippians hearing of his illness. Nothing is said here about a sentence.

Careful, baker, this one has a catch. Paul says, "…God had mercy on him, and not only on him but also on me, to spare me sorrow upon sorrow." (Philippians 2:27) So the mercy reached Paul too. Epaphroditus wasn't the only one.

That's right. Paul says, "…God had mercy on him, and not only on him but also on me, to spare me sorrow upon sorrow." (Philippians 2:27) Epaphroditus got mercy, and so did Paul. The mercy didn't stop at one man.

Yes, baker! Paul says he's eager to send Epaphroditus "…so that when you see him again you may rejoice, and I may be less anxious." (Philippians 2:28) The Philippians may rejoice, and Paul may be less anxious. I think everybody sleeps better once a friend is home.

It's a natural guess, friend, but that's not Paul's word. He says he wants the Philippians to rejoice, "…and I may be less anxious." (Philippians 2:28) The word is anxious. Paul doesn't say lonely there.

Timothy is in this passage, friend, but he isn't what Epaphroditus nearly died for. Paul says, "…he nearly died for the work of Christ…" (Philippians 2:30) The work of Christ is the reason Paul gives.
